--- title: "Pandas" subtitle: Manipulating tables author: Dr. Yu Cheng Hsu title-slide-attributes: data-background: /assets/images/functional-genomics/background-1.jpg data-background-size: 40% 100% data-background-position: right data-background-opacity: "0.8" format: revealjs: theme: [default, ../../../assets/css/general_style.css] slide-number: true smaller: true lightbox: true chalkboard: theme: whiteboard src: None engine: Jupyter bibliography: ref.bib lightbox: true --- ## Learning Objectives - Perform table manipulation with pandas - Evaluate the code robustness and its implication - Appreciate and apply pipeline mindset :::{.aside} Background image: @bg1 ::: ## Library In python a lot of developer will write their own code and share to other to reuse. This package of code are called `library` To install a specific library you can do ::: {#00dff26b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} ! pip install PACKAGE_NAME ``` ::: You do not need to do this on Google colab as Google colab pre-installed most of the commonly used package for you already **Import library** You can import the installed library throgh keyword `import` ## Pandas ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - Pandas is a specialized library for manipulating tabular data - To use the exisiting library we can do ::: {#3c6cbfed .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 'pd' is the universal standard nickname for pandas. # Every coder in the world uses this exact line. import pandas as pd ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column} **Dataset Overview** You will analyze brain tissue RNA-Seq profiles from mice infected with influenza over an 8-day timecourse: * **Source:** [link](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/uclouvain-cbio/WSBIM1207/master/data/rnaseq.csv) * **Key columns:** `gene`, `sample`, `expression`, `sex`, `infection`, `time`, `tissue`, `gene_biotype` The case is adopted from @laurent_gatto_2021_5532658 with data from @blackmore2017influenza ::: ::: ## Loading the data - Data table is called a DataFrame (usually abbreviated as `df`) in Pandas - To read the data we use `pd.read_csv("FILE_LOCATION")` ::: {#c287116c .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Load the CSV file into memory # (Assume we uploaded 'rnaseq_results.csv' to Colab) df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UCLouvain-CBIO/WSBIM1207/refs/heads/main/docs/data/rnaseq.csv") # Printing the first 3 rows fo the dataframe print(df.head(5)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gene sample expression organism age sex infection \ 0 Asl GSM2545336 1170 Mus musculus 8 Female InfluenzaA 1 Apod GSM2545336 36194 Mus musculus 8 Female InfluenzaA 2 Cyp2d22 GSM2545336 4060 Mus musculus 8 Female InfluenzaA 3 Klk6 GSM2545336 287 Mus musculus 8 Female InfluenzaA 4 Fcrls GSM2545336 85 Mus musculus 8 Female InfluenzaA strain time tissue mouse ENTREZID \ 0 C57BL/6 8 Cerebellum 14 109900 1 C57BL/6 8 Cerebellum 14 11815 2 C57BL/6 8 Cerebellum 14 56448 3 C57BL/6 8 Cerebellum 14 19144 4 C57BL/6 8 Cerebellum 14 80891 product ensembl_gene_id \ 0 argininosuccinate lyase, transcript variant X1 ENSMUSG00000025533 1 apolipoprotein D, transcript variant 3 ENSMUSG00000022548 2 cytochrome P450, family 2, subfamily d, polype... ENSMUSG00000015852 external_synonym chromosome_name gene_biotype \ 0 2510006M18Rik 5 protein_coding 1 NaN 16 protein_coding 2 2D22 15 protein_coding 3 Bssp 7 protein_coding 4 2810439C17Rik 3 protein_coding phenotype_description \ 0 abnormal circulating amino acid level 1 abnormal lipid homeostasis 2 abnormal skin morphology 3 abnormal cytokine level 4 decreased CD8-positive alpha-beta T cell number hsapiens_homolog_associated_gene_name 0 ASL 1 APOD 2 CYP2D6 3 KLK6 4 FCRL2 ``` ::: ::: ## Inspecting the DataFrame Some few information you can retrieved of your data - `.shape` : The dimensions: (number_of_rows, number_of_columns) - `.columns` : List of all the column headers ::: {#a9f923c7 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 1. df.shape tells you the dimensions: (number_of_rows, number_of_columns) print("Data dimensions:", df.shape) # 2. df.columns gives you a List of all the column headers print("Column names:", df.columns) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Data dimensions: (32428, 19) Column names: Index(['gene', 'sample', 'expression', 'organism', 'age', 'sex', 'infection', 'strain', 'time', 'tissue', 'mouse', 'ENTREZID', 'product', 'ensembl_gene_id', 'external_synonym', 'chromosome_name', 'gene_biotype', 'phenotype_description', 'hsapiens_homolog_associated_gene_name'], dtype='object') ``` ::: ::: ## Selecting Columns Subset the DataFrame by passing a `List` of the column names you want to keep inside square brackets. ::: {#ad72ee82 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} # We use double brackets: the outer brackets are for Pandas, # and the inner brackets represent our Python List of names! df_subset = df[["gene", "expression", "tissue"]] df_subset.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## Precise Slicing `.loc` and `.iloc` ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} **`.loc` Label location** ::: {#ef67aa5b .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 1. Turn the "gene" column into the Index df_indexed = df.set_index("gene") # 2. Let's find the data for the Plp1 gene: plp1_data = df_indexed.loc["Plp1", :] print("Data for Plp1:") print(plp1_data.head(2)) # 3. We can be highly specific: # "Give me the Plp1 row, but only the expression column" plp1_exp = df_indexed.loc["Plp1", "expression"] print("Plp1 Expression:", plp1_exp.head(2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Data for Plp1: sample expression organism age sex infection strain \ gene Plp1 GSM2545336 43217 Mus musculus 8 Female InfluenzaA C57BL/6 Plp1 GSM2545337 101241 Mus musculus 8 Female NonInfected C57BL/6 time tissue mouse ENTREZID \ gene Plp1 8 Cerebellum 14 18823 Plp1 0 Cerebellum 9 18823 product ensembl_gene_id \ gene Plp1 proteolipid protein (myelin) 1, transcript var... ENSMUSG00000031425 Plp1 proteolipid protein (myelin) 1, transcript var... ENSMUSG00000031425 external_synonym chromosome_name gene_biotype \ gene Plp1 DM20 X protein_coding Plp1 DM20 X protein_coding phenotype_description hsapiens_homolog_associated_gene_name gene Plp1 abnormal CNS glial cell morphology PLP1 Plp1 abnormal CNS glial cell morphology PLP1 Plp1 Expression: gene Plp1 43217 Plp1 101241 Name: expression, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} **`.iloc` index location** ::: {#dcebbdef .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Grab the first row (index 0) and all columns (the colon :) first_row = df.iloc[0, :] # Grab the first 3 rows, and only the first 2 columns # (Remember: 0:3 means it grabs 0, 1, and 2. It stops BEFORE 3!) top_left_block = df.iloc[0:3, 0:2] print(top_left_block) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` gene sample 0 Asl GSM2545336 1 Apod GSM2545336 2 Cyp2d22 GSM2545336 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Comparison | Feature | .iloc (Integer Location) | .loc (Label Location) | |---------|-------------------------------------------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------| | Lookup Mechanism | **Position-based**: Uses exact numerical coordinates (0, 1, 2). | **Name-based**: Uses the actual row/column names. | | Example Syntax | `df.iloc[0:5, 2]` | `df.loc["BRCA1":"EGFR", "expression"] ` | | Slicing Rule | **Exclusive** of the stop number (`0:3` grabs 0, 1, 2). | **Inclusive** of the stop name (`"A":"C"` grabs A, B, and C). | | Best Used For | Grabbing the "Top 10" rows, or dealing with un-named data. | Extracting specific genes, writing reproducible pipelines. | | Robustness | **Highly Fragile**. Breaks silently if data changes. | **Highly Robust**. Immune to structural column/row shifts. | ## Robustness matters Goal: Extracting the `expression` column ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} **`.loc` Label location** - Use actual name ::: {#afa62f3e .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Extract all rows for the `expression` column df.loc[:, "expression"].head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` 0 1170 1 36194 2 4060 Name: expression, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column} **`.iloc` index location** ::: {#0a08627b .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Extract all rows for the 3rd column df.iloc[:, 2].head(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 0 1170 1 36194 2 4060 Name: expression, dtype: int64 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: **Scenario**: Sequencing facility updates their software and adds a new `quality_score` column at the very beginning of the CSV. What will happen ? - label location: Not affected - index location: Not referring to the intended column (and without warning message) ## Creating new columns Creating new column: - Assign on a new column. - Do not need to loop all cells, Most of the python math function will apply the math mfunctin to every cells in the table ::: {#30f701af .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} #### Time start (This is for the next slides) start_time_loop = time.time() ## Exact code starts # Create a new column called 'log_expression' df["log_expression"] = np.log2(df["expression"]) #### Exact code ends, Below are for the next slides and display purpose end_time_loop = time.time() loop_time = end_time_loop - start_time_loop print(f"For loop finished in: {loop_time:.5f} seconds") df.head(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` For loop finished in: 0.00116 seconds ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ## What if using `for` Loops We can use for loop to achieve exactly the same goal ::: {#befbee9f .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Time start start_time_loop = time.time() #### Exact code starts here # 1. Create an empty list to store the answers new_values = [] # 2. Loop through every single row in the dataframe for i in range(len(df)): # Calculate the new value for this specific row and appe math_result = np.log2(df.loc[i, "expression"]) new_values.append(math_result) # 3. Assign the completed list as a new column df["log_expression"] = new_values #### Exact code ends, Time end end_time_loop = time.time() loop_time = end_time_loop - start_time_loop print(f"For loop finished in: {loop_time:.2f} seconds") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` For loop finished in: 0.15 seconds ``` ::: ::: ## Advantage of using `Pandas` ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} **Vectorization** (Pandas) - Code Clarity: Poor. Using 5 lines to write - Time efficiency: Low (0.16s) ::: ::: {.column} **`For` loop** (Pandas) - Code Clarity: Great. 1 line solution, easy to understand - Time efficiency: Fast (0.001s) ::: ::: - The time difference will be more prominent when the rows increase ## Save your results `.to_csv`/ `.to_excel` methods can let you save your results ::: {#614f8408 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Save our filtered 'highly_expressed_genes' table to a new CSV file. # index=False prevents Pandas from exporting the 0,1,2,3 row numbers. df.to_csv("high_expression_results.csv", index=False) ``` ::: # Data wrangling ## Motivations If we manipulate the data with what we have just cover ::: {#7abfe809 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} # Create a copy of df to prevent overwriting my_data = df.copy() # 2. Filter for high expression my_data = my_data[my_data["expression"] > 50000] # 3. Talking the log of expression my_data["expression"] = np.log2(my_data["expression"]) ``` ::: **Problems** Colab lets you run the same cell multiple times (by accidentally pressing Shift + Enter twice), this step-by-step approach is highly dangerous. - Run 1: Your expression of 60,000 is taking log to log(60000) - Run 2: You accidentally run the cell again. Python take log again become log(log(60000)) ## Other problem The below code will give you a warning ::: {#cf141128 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} # 1. Filter the data high_exp = df[df["expression"] > 50000] # 2. Try to do math on the filtered data high_exp["expression_k"] = high_exp["expression"] / 1000 ``` ::: Pandas gives you warning because it isn't sure if high_exp is a brand-new table or just a "window" looking at the original `df` **Implication** If between the step 1 and 2 you do some change on `df["expression"]`, `high_exp` won't get the updated value ## Method chaining In stead of this messy way, `Pandas' provide a **method chaining** approach to make your code clearer. In specific, we will focus on the following methods ::: {.columns} ::: {.column} - `.query()`: Selecting data - `.assign()`: Adding new column - `.groupby()`: Group data by the designated group - `.agg()`: calculate summary statistics ::: ::: {.column} **Example** ::: {#58bb76b2 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The parentheses () tell Python this is one pipeline. final_df = ( df # 1. FILTER: Keep only high expression .query("expression > 50000") # 2. MUTATE: Create a BRAND NEW column .assign( log_exp = lambda x: np.log(x["expression"] + 1)) # 3. SELECT: Keep only these three columns at the very end [["gene", "sample", "log_exp"]] ) ``` ::: ::: ::: ## `.query()`: Filtering Rows `.query()` lets you write the filtering condition as a clean string. ::: {#cd4da430 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} df.query("expression > 50000 and tissue == 'Cerebellum'").head(1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}
gene sample expression organism age sex infection strain time tissue mouse ENTREZID product ensembl_gene_id external_synonym chromosome_name gene_biotype phenotype_description hsapiens_homolog_associated_gene_name log_expression
50 Glul GSM2545336 89445 Mus musculus 8 Female InfluenzaA C57BL/6 8 Cerebellum 14 14645 glutamate-ammonia ligase (glutamine synthetase) ENSMUSG00000026473 Glns 1 protein_coding embryonic lethality before implantation incomp... GLUL 16.448713
``` ::: ::: - Quotes inside quotes: If the outer query uses double quotes `"..."`, use single quotes `'...'` for text values inside (like `'Cerebellum'`). - Natural logic: You can write `and` / `or` - Using external variables: Prefix a Python variable with `@` to reference it inside the query string ::: {#0bac4eb2 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} cutoff=50000 df.query("expression > @cutoff") ``` ::: ## `.assign()`: Creating or Modifying Columns `.assign()`adds new columns and returns a new DataFrame without modifying the original rna table. ::: {#d1bf205f .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The parentheses () tell Python this is one pipeline. final_df = ( df .assign( time_hours = lambda x: x["time"] * 24, time_min = lambda x: x["time_hours"] * 60, log_exp = lambda x: np.log(x["expression"] + 1) ) ) ``` ::: - `lambda x:` : `x` represents the current state of the DataFrame at that exact step. If you filtered rows in the line above, `lambda x:` ensures you are calculating on the filtered data. - Sequential creation: you can reference a column you just created in the very next line of the same `.assign()` call ## `.agg()`: summarize data `.agg()` (aggregate) computes summary statistics for each group ::: {#d0dbceea .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} # The parentheses () tell Python this is one pipeline. ( df .agg( mean_expression = ("expression", "mean"), median_expression = ("expression", "median"), n_samples = ("sample", "count") ) .reset_index() ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}
index expression sample
0 mean_expression 1860.362619 NaN
1 median_expression 547.000000 NaN
2 n_samples NaN 32428.0
``` ::: ::: - Named Aggregation syntax:`new_col_name = ("source_column", "stat_function")` - Always finish with `.reset_index()`: By default, `.groupby()` turns your grouping variables (gene, infection, time) into a nested row Index. Adding .reset_index() flattens them back into regular columns ## Bibliography Notes
